### Problem `#062` — AtCoder ARC 106 E: Medals (Binary Search + SOS DP Hall Elimination)

- **Canonical Slot**: `Ch 08 — Advanced 2 (Adv-2)` | **Judge URL**: [AtCoder ARC 106 E](https://atcoder.jp/contests/arc106/tasks/arc106_e) *(Companions: [ARC 076 F — Exhausted?](https://atcoder.jp/contests/arc076/tasks/arc076_f) & [CF 981 F — Round Marriage](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/981/F))*
- **Constraints**: $1 \le N \le 18$ employees, $1 \le K \le 10^5$ medals per employee, shift lengths $1 \le A_i \le 10^5$, Time Limit $2.5\text{ s}$.
- **Problem Statement**: $N \le 18$ employees each need $K \le 10^5$ medals. Employee $i$ works for $A_i$ consecutive days, then rests for $A_i$ consecutive days, then works for $A_i$ days, and so on (so on day $t \ge 1$, employee $i$ is at work iff $\lfloor (t - 1) / A_i \rfloor$ is even). On each day, you may award **at most $1$ medal** to one employee who is at work that day. Find the minimum number of days $D$ required so that all $N$ employees can receive $K$ medals each.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Upper Bound on $D$ & Binary Search Monotonicity"}
Because each employee works at least half of all days (specifically, out of every $2 A_i$ days they work $A_i$ days), within $D_{\max} = 2 N K \le 3.6 \cdot 10^6$ days, at least $N K$ work-days exist even if we served employees one by one! Moreover, if $D$ days suffice, then $D + 1$ days also suffice—so we can **binary search on $D \in [N K, 2 N K]$**!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Hall's Marriage Theorem on $N \le 18$ Employees vs. $D$ Days"}
For a candidate deadline $D$, we have a bipartite supply–demand graph between $L = \{0, \dots, N-1\}$ (each needing $K$ medals) and $R = \{1, \dots, D\}$ (each day supplying $1$ medal). By **Hall's Theorem** (Theorem 3.1(2)), a valid assignment exists iff for every subset $S \subseteq L$ ($2^N$ subsets), the number of days in $[1, D]$ where **at least one** employee in $S$ works is $\ge K \cdot |S|$.
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Counting Disjoint Days via Complement Fast Zeta Transform (SOS DP)"}
For each day $t \in [1, 2NK]$, precompute the $N$-bit mask `mask[t]` of employees working on day $t$. Inside the binary search for $D$, how many days $t \in [1, D]$ have `mask[t]` intersecting $S$ ($\text{mask}[t] \cap S \neq \emptyset$)? By Theorem 3.1(3), it equals $D$ minus the number of days where $\text{mask}[t] \subseteq L \setminus S$, which is computed for all $2^N$ masks simultaneously in $O(N 2^N)$ via **SOS DP (Fast Zeta Transform)**!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — #062 (ARC 106 E)"}
#### Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
$N \le 18$ on the left and $D \le 3.6 \cdot 10^6$ on the right: explicit Dinic on $3.6 \cdot 10^6$ vertices is impossible, while $2^{18} = 262,144$ is tiny! This is the canonical trigger for **Engine 4 (`Section 4.2`): Binary Search + Complement SOS DP Hall Elimination**.

#### Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
Let $m_t \in [0, 2^N)$ be the bitmask of employees working on day $t \in \{1, \dots, D\}$. For any subset $S \subseteq \{0, \dots, N-1\}$, the neighborhood size $|N(S)|$ in $[1, D]$ is:

$$|N(S)| = \#\big\{t \in [1, D] : m_t \cap S \neq \emptyset\big\} = D - \#\big\{t \in [1, D] : m_t \subseteq \bar{S}\big\} = D - g[\bar{S}],$$

where $\bar{S} = (2^N - 1) \oplus S$ and $g[T] := \sum_{M \subseteq T} \text{cnt}_D[M]$ is the upward subset-sum of frequency array $\text{cnt}_D[M] = \#\{t \in [1, D] : m_t = M\}$. By Hall's Theorem, $D$ is feasible iff:

$$\forall S \in [1, 2^N), \qquad D - g\big[(2^N - 1) \oplus S\big] \ge K \cdot \text{popcount}(S).$$

#### Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Compilation)
1. Precompute `mask[t]` for $t = 1, \dots, 2NK$ **once** outside the binary search in $O(N \cdot NK)$ time by toggling bit $i$ every $A_i$ days (avoiding slow `%` division in the inner loop!).
2. Binary search $D \in [NK, 2NK]$ ($\approx 22$ iterations):
   - Zero-fill $g[0 \dots 2^N - 1]$, and for $t = 1 \dots D$, increment $g[\text{mask}[t]]$.
   - Run Fast Zeta Transform: for $i = 0 \dots N-1$, for $T = 0 \dots 2^N - 1$, if $(T \gg i) \ \& \ 1$, do $g[T] += g[T \oplus (1 \ll i)]$.
   - Check $D - g[(2^N - 1) \oplus S] \ge K \cdot \text{popcount}(S)$ for all $S$.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
- **Toy Trace**: $N = 2, K = 1, A = [1, 2]$.
  - Day 1: both work ($m_1 = 3$). Day 2: only emp 1 ($A_1=2$) works ($m_2 = 2$).
  - At $D = 2$: $\text{cnt}[3] = 1, \text{cnt}[2] = 1$. For $S = \{0, 1\} = 3$, $\bar{S} = 0$, $g[0] = 0 \implies 2 - 0 \ge 2$ (OK). For $S = \{0\} = 1$, $\bar{S} = 2$, $g[2] = \text{cnt}[0] + \text{cnt}[2] = 1 \implies 2 - 1 = 1 \ge 1$ (OK). So $D = 2$ is feasible!
- **Failure-Mode Guard**: Never recompute `mask[t]` using `(t - 1) / A[i] % 2` inside the binary search! Precomputing `mask[1 .. 2NK]` before the binary search cuts the runtime from TLE ($> 3\text{ s}$) to $250\text{ ms}$. Complexity: $O(N^2 K + N 2^N \log(NK))$.

```cpp
// O(N^2 K + N 2^N log(NK)) SOS DP Hall Solver for #062 (ARC 106 E — Medals)
int solve_medals(int N, int K, const vector<int>& A) {
    int MAXD = 2 * N * K;
    vector<int> mask(MAXD + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        for (int start = 1; start <= MAXD; start += 2 * A[i]) {
            int end_day = min(MAXD, start + A[i] - 1);
            for (int t = start; t <= end_day; ++t) mask[t] |= (1 << i);
        }
    }
    int full_mask = (1 << N) - 1;
    vector<int> g(1 << N);
    auto check = [&](int D) {
        fill(g.begin(), g.end(), 0);
        for (int t = 1; t <= D; ++t) g[mask[t]]++;
        for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i)
            for (int T = 0; T <= full_mask; ++T)
                if ((T >> i) & 1) g[T] += g[T ^ (1 << i)];
        for (int S = 1; S <= full_mask; ++S)
            if (D - g[full_mask ^ S] < K * __builtin_popcount(S)) return false;
        return true;
    };
    int lo = N * K, hi = MAXD;
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (check(mid)) hi = mid;
        else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;
}
```

### Problem `#063` — CF 590 E: Birthday (Aho–Corasick Fail-Tree Compression + Dilworth Antichain)

- **Canonical Slot**: `Ch 08 — Mastery 1 (Mas-1)` | **Judge URL**: [Codeforces 590E](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/590/E)
- **Constraints**: $1 \le N \le 750$ binary strings over `'a'`, `'b'`, total length $\sum_{i=1}^N |S_i| \le 10^7$, Time Limit $3.0\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $512\text{ MB}$.
- **Problem Statement**: You are given $N \le 750$ distinct ribbons (strings of `'a'` and `'b'`) of total length up to $10^7$. Select the maximum possible number of ribbons such that **no selected ribbon is a contiguous substring of another selected ribbon**, and print the $1$-based indices of the chosen ribbons.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Poset Formulation & Why Naive Substring Graph Building TLEs"}
Define the strict substring poset $i \prec j \iff (i \neq j \land S_i \text{ is a substring of } S_j)$. We want a **Maximum Antichain** of $(V, \prec)$, which takes $O(N^3 / 64 + N^{2.5})$ once we have the poset! However, if we walk the Aho–Corasick automaton along $S_j$ and traverse all fail-links at every prefix of $S_j$, we could visit $O(N)$ matched substrings per character, taking $O(N \sum |S_j|) \approx 7.5 \cdot 10^9$ operations (TLE)!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Compressing the Aho–Corasick Fail-Tree to Immediate Ancestors"}
Because we will compute the **transitive closure** on the $N \times N$ graph anyway (via Floyd–Warshall), at each prefix node $u$ of string $S_j$, we do **not** need to add edges from $j$ to *all* pattern strings on $u$'s fail-chain! We only need to add a single directed edge from $j$ to the **longest proper substring pattern** ending at $u$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Path-Compressed `nearest_pat[u]` + Bitset Floyd–Warshall + Lemma 2.1"}
During the Aho–Corasick BFS, maintain `nearest_pat[u]` = the pattern ID at node $u$ if $u$ is a pattern terminal, else `nearest_pat[fail[u]]`. Then for each string $S_j$ and each prefix node $u$ of $S_j$, add edge $j \to \text{nearest\_pat}[u]$ (or $\text{nearest\_pat}[\text{fail}[u]]$ at the final node of $S_j$ so $j$ doesn't add a self-loop $j \to j$). Finally, close transitively with `std::bitset<750>` and extract $A^* = \{i : i_{\text{out}} \in S_{\min} \land i_{\text{in}} \notin S_{\min}\}$!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — #063 (CF 590 E — Birthday)"}
#### Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
"No selected string is a substring of another" is **Maximum Antichain in the Substring Poset**. The twin challenges are:

1. Compressing $O(\sum |S_i|) = 10^7$ Aho–Corasick substring relationships into an $N \times N$ ($750 \times 750$) DAG using **only $O(1)$ work per character** by delegating transitivity to the $O(N^3 / w)$ bitset Floyd–Warshall phase!
2. Extracting the explicit antichain via **Lemma 2.1 (`vis_S[u] && !vis_S[u + N]`)**.

#### Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For any prefix node $u$ of string $S_j$, let $p(u)$ be the longest pattern $S_i$ ($i \neq j$) that is a suffix of the prefix represented by $u$. Any shorter pattern $S_k$ that is also a suffix of $u$ is necessarily a suffix (hence substring) of $S_i$! Thus:

$$S_k \preceq_{\text{suffix}} u \iff S_k \preceq_{\text{suffix}} S_i \preceq_{\text{suffix}} u.$$

Adding only the single Hasse-like edge $j \to i$ at each prefix of $S_j$ preserves the exact same **transitive closure** $\text{TC}(G)$ on $\{1, \dots, N\}$!

#### Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Compilation)

1. Insert all $N$ strings into a flat-array Aho–Corasick trie (`ch[MAXL][2]`, `term_id[MAXL]`).
2. In the BFS computing `fail[u]`, propagate `nearest_pat[u] = term_id[u] ? term_id[u] : nearest_pat[fail[u]]`.
3. Walk each string $S_j$ in the trie: at each node $u$ along $S_j$, let `p = (u == end_node[j]) ? nearest_pat[fail[u]] : nearest_pat[u]`. If `p != 0`, set `reach[j][p] = 1`.
4. Run $O(N^3 / 64)$ `std::bitset<750>` Floyd–Warshall on `reach`, run Hopcroft–Karp / Dinic on $G_{\text{split}}(\text{reach})$, and extract $A^* = \{i : \text{vis\_S}[i] \land \neg\text{vis\_S}[i + N]\}$.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard

- **Toy Trace**: $S_1 = \text{"a"}$, $S_2 = \text{"ab"}$, $S_3 = \text{"bab"}$.
  - Walking $S_3 = \text{"bab"}$: at prefix `"ba"`, `nearest_pat` is $S_1 (\text{"a"})$, adding $3 \to 1$. At full string `"bab"`, `nearest_pat[fail["bab"]]` is $S_2 (\text{"ab"})$, adding $3 \to 2$. Walking $S_2 = \text{"ab"}$ adds $2 \to 1$.
  - Notice that even if `"bab"` hadn't directly touched $S_1$, $3 \to 2$ and $2 \to 1$ close transitively to $3 \to 1$!
- **Failure-Mode Guard**: With $\sum |S_i| = 10^7$ and a $512\text{ MB}$ limit, never use `std::vector` per trie node! Use flat 32-bit `int` arrays `ch[MAXL][2]`, `fail[MAXL]`, and `nearest_pat[MAXL]` ($\approx 160\text{ MB}$ total).


### Problem `#064` — CF 1089 B: Guests (Tutte's 2-for-1 Twin Gadget & General Graph Blossom Matching)

- **Canonical Slot**: `Ch 08 — Mastery 2 (Mas-2)` | **Judge URL**: [Codeforces 1089B](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1089/B)
- **Constraints**: $T$ test cases, $1 \le N, M \le 150$ ($N$ guests, $M$ bedrooms), $\sum (N + M) \le 600$, Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$.
- **Problem Statement**: A hotel has $N \le 150$ guests and $M \le 150$ two-bed bedrooms. You are given the bipartite preference matrix between guests and bedrooms. Two guests can be paired into a bedroom $r$ if and only if **both** guests like bedroom $r$ (each bedroom can hold at most one pair of guests, and each guest can be assigned to at most one bedroom). Maximize the total number of **guest pairs** formed.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Why Bipartite Flow Cannot Enforce '2 Guests or 0 Guests'"}
If we simply give each bedroom $r$ a sink capacity of $c(r, T) = 2$ in a bipartite flow network, the max-flow solver will happily send **$1$ unit of flow** into bedroom $r$ (assigning a single unpaired guest to $r$) and count it toward the total flow! We need bedroom $r$ to contribute $+1$ to the objective **only when $2$ guests** are matched to it, and **$0$ net gain** when $0$ or $1$ guest is matched to it!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Tutte's 2-for-1 Twin Gadget (`r_1 — r_2` Internal Edge)"}
Split each bedroom $r \in \{1, \dots, M\}$ into **two** bed vertices $r_1$ and $r_2$, and connect them with an **internal edge $(r_1, r_2)$**! Connect every guest $g$ who likes room $r$ to **both** $r_1$ and $r_2$. Now analyze how many matched edges are Incident to $\{r_1, r_2\}$ in any maximum matching of this general graph!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Counting the Net Matching Gain & Edmonds' Blossom Algorithm"}
In the general graph on $N + 2M$ vertices:

- If **$0$ guests** match to $\{r_1, r_2\}$, the internal edge $(r_1, r_2)$ matches with itself: **$1$ matched edge**.
- If **$1$ guest** $g$ matches to $r_1$, then $(r_1, r_2)$ is broken and $r_2$ is left unmatched: still **$1$ matched edge** ($0$ net gain!).
- If **$2$ guests** $g_a, g_b$ match to $r_1$ and $r_2$, we get **$2$ matched edges** ($+1$ net gain over the baseline!).

Therefore, $\text{MaxGeneralMatching}(G) - M$ equals the **exact** maximum number of guest pairs!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Full 4-Step Compilation & Solution — #064 (CF 1089 B — Guests)"}
#### Step 1: Non-Graph Diagnostic Signal (Recognition)
At first sight, "guests and bedrooms" looks bipartite. However, the objective pairs **two guests $g_a, g_b \in L$** through a shared bedroom $r \in R$. This is a **capacitated parity / 2-for-1 packing problem** ($N, M \le 150$), which crosses the boundary from Bipartite Matching into **General Graph Matching (Edmonds' Blossom Algorithm)** via **Tutte's Twin-Clique Gadget**.

#### Step 2: Intermediate Algebraic Representation
For each bedroom $r \in \{1, \dots, M\}$, let $k_r \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ be the number of guests assigned to room $r$. We want to maximize $\sum_{r=1}^M \lfloor k_r / 2 \rfloor$.
Notice the algebraic identity for $k_r \in \{0, 1, 2\}$:

$$1 + \left\lfloor \frac{k_r}{2} \right\rfloor = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } k_r = 0, \\ 1 & \text{if } k_r = 1, \\ 2 & \text{if } k_r = 2. \end{cases}$$

How can a vertex pair $\{r_1, r_2\}$ contribute $1$ to the matching size when $k_r \in \{0, 1\}$ and $2$ when $k_r = 2$? By placing an edge $(r_1, r_2)$ between them! When $k_r = 0$, $(r_1, r_2)$ is matched ($+1$); when $k_r = 1$, one guest matches to $r_1$ and $(r_1, r_2)$ is unmatched ($+1$); when $k_r = 2$, two guests match to $r_1$ and $r_2$ ($+2$). Summing over all $M$ bedrooms yields:

$$\nu(G_{\text{twin}}) = \sum_{r=1}^M \left(1 + \left\lfloor \frac{k_r}{2} \right\rfloor\right) = M + \sum_{r=1}^M \left\lfloor \frac{k_r}{2} \right\rfloor \implies \max \text{Pairs} = \nu(G_{\text{twin}}) - M.$$

#### Step 3: Reverse-Engineering Scratchpad (Mechanical Graph Compilation)
- Create a general undirected graph $G_{\text{twin}}$ with $V = N + 2M \le 450$ vertices:
  - Guests are $0, \dots, N - 1$.
  - Bedroom $r \in \{0, \dots, M - 1\}$ has twin vertices $r_1 = N + 2r$ and $r_2 = N + 2r + 1$, connected by internal edge $(r_1, r_2)$.
  - If guest $g$ likes bedroom $r$, add undirected edges $(g, r_1)$ and $(g, r_2)$.
- Run **Edmonds' Blossom Algorithm** in $O(V^3)$ time to compute $\nu(G_{\text{twin}})$, and output $\nu(G_{\text{twin}}) - M$.

#### Step 4: Hand-Checkable Toy Trace & Failure-Mode Guard
- **Toy Trace**: $N = 3$ guests $\{g_1, g_2, g_3\}$, $M = 2$ rooms $\{r, s\}$. $g_1, g_2$ like $r$; $g_3$ likes $s$.
  - In Room $r$: $g_1$ matches $r_1$, $g_2$ matches $r_2$ ($2$ edges).
  - In Room $s$: even if $g_3$ matches $s_1$ (or $(s_1, s_2)$ stays matched), Room $s$ contributes only $1$ edge!
  - Total matching $\nu(G_{\text{twin}}) = 2 + 1 = 3$, and $\nu - M = 3 - 2 = \mathbf{1}$ guest pair.
- **Failure-Mode Guard**: Notice that $(g, r_1, r_2)$ forms a **3-cycle (odd cycle / blossom)**! Running a bipartite matching solver on $G_{\text{twin}}$ is completely invalid—you **must** contract odd cycles via Edmonds' Blossom algorithm (or compute $\text{rank}(A_{\text{Tutte}}) / 2 - M$ modulo $998244353$).

```cpp
// Graph Compilation for #064 (CF 1089 B — Guests) using Blossom Solver
int solve_guests(int N, int M, const vector<string>& likes) {
    int V = N + 2 * M;
    BlossomMatcher blossom(V); // Standard O(V^3) Edmonds Blossom template
    for (int r = 0; r < M; ++r) {
        int r1 = N + 2 * r, r2 = N + 2 * r + 1;
        blossom.add_edge(r1, r2); // Internal twin edge (baseline +1 per room)
        for (int g = 0; g < N; ++g) {
            if (likes[g][r] == '1') {
                blossom.add_edge(g, r1);
                blossom.add_edge(g, r2);
            }
        }
    }
    return blossom.max_matching() - M;
}
```

## 7. Chapter 8 Verification Checklist, Failure Mode Summary & Blind Checkpoint `CP-II`

### 7.1 Pre-Submission Verification Checklist (`FM-08` & Hall Guards)

Before submitting any DAG Path Cover, Poset Antichain, or Hall Flow-Elimination solution, run through these five structural checks:

1. **Disjoint vs. Overlapping Path Cover (`FM-08` Part 1)**: Can two paths share an intermediate vertex? If **yes** (or if you are finding an antichain of a reachability poset), did you compute the **Transitive Closure** $\text{TC}(G)$ (with zero diagonal `reach[u][u] = 0`) *before* building $G_{\text{split}}$?
2. **`AND` vs. `OR` in Constructive Antichain Recovery (`FM-08` Part 2 / `H-06`)**: When extracting a Maximum Antichain from the residual reachability set $S_{\min}$ of $G_{\text{split}}(\text{TC}(G))$, did you require **both** $v_{\text{out}} \notin C^*$ and $v_{\text{in}} \notin C^*$, i.e., `vis_S[v_out] && !vis_S[v_in]`?
3. **Feasibility ($\le 0$) vs. Positive Defect ($> 0$) on Contiguous Intervals (Lemma 4.1)**:
   - If testing **feasibility** ($\text{def}(I) \le 0$), checking single intervals $[l, r]$ is 100% exact (`POI 2009 LYZ`, `CF 981 F`).
   - If computing **positive maximum defect** ($\nu(G) < \sum a_u$) for interior intervals $N(u) = [l_u, r_u]$, did you use multi-interval DP $dp[r] = \max(dp[r-1], \max_l (dp[l-2] + \text{def}([l, r])))$ instead of a single interval? (For prefix–suffix unions $[1, L_u] \cup [R_u, M]$ in `ARC 076 F`, the complement $(L_u, R_u)$ is contiguous, so a single $(L, R)$ query in a Lazy Segment Tree is exact!)
4. **Complement Direction in SOS DP (`ARC 106 E`, `CF 1009 G`)**: In Theorem 3.1(3), $|N(S)| = |R| - g[L \setminus S]$ where $g[T] = \sum_{M \subseteq T} \text{cnt}[M]$ sums over **subsets** of $T = L \setminus S$ (not supersets!).
5. **Cycles vs. Trees in Hyperedge Realization (`AGC 029 F`)**: Finding a perfect matching between $N - 1$ hyperedges and $V \setminus \{1\}$ is necessary but **not sufficient** for tree connectivity; did you run the alternating BFS from root $1$ (`u -> incident e -> match_v[e]`) and verify `visited_count == N`?

### 7.2 Part II Mastery: Two-Stage Blind Diagnostic Checkpoint (`CP-II`: `#201`–`#208`)

In a real contest, problems do not come labeled with chapter numbers. Test your Part II recognition reflexes on these **8 scrambled problem statements** (5 genuine flow/matching/Hall problems from Chapters 5–8 + 3 non-flow decoys):

- **`#201` (`CP-II-1`)**: Given $N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ brides and $N$ grooms on a circle of circumference $L$, minimize the maximum circular distance between matched pairs.
- **`#202` (`CP-II-2`)**: Given a tree $T = (V, E)$ with vertex weights $w_v > 0$ ($N \le 2 \cdot 10^5$), select a maximum-weight independent set of vertices.
- **`#203` (`CP-II-3`)**: Given a DAG with $N \le 200$ vertices where each vertex $v$ must be visited by at least $1$ and at most $c_v$ paths, minimize the number of paths needed to cover all vertices.
- **`#204` (`CP-II-4`)**: Given $N \le 3000$ integers $a_1, \dots, a_N$, select the maximum-size subset such that no two selected integers satisfy $a_i + a_j = 2^k$ for any integer $k \ge 1$.
- **`#205` (`CP-II-5`)**: Given $N \le 500$ intervals $[l_i, r_i]$ with weights $w_i > 0$, select a subset of **pairwise overlapping** intervals of maximum total weight.
- **`#206` (`CP-II-6`)**: Two players play on an $N \times M$ grid ($N, M \le 100$) where a token starts at $(r_0, c_0)$ and moves to an orthogonal neighbor $(r', c')$ with strictly larger value $A_{r', c'} > A_{r, c}$. Determine if the first player has a winning strategy.
- **`#207` (`CP-II-7`)**: Given an $N \times M$ board ($N, M \le 50$) where lasers can be placed on `.` cells and shoot until hitting `#` walls (passing harmlessly through `x` pits), place the maximum number of mutually non-attacking lasers **and** output all `.` cells that *must* contain a laser in every optimal placement.
- **`#208` (`CP-II-8`)**: Given a bipartite graph $G = (L \sqcup R, E)$ ($|L|, |R| \le 500$) with vertex weights $w_v > 0$, find a minimum-weight subset of vertices covering every edge, and output the subset.

## 8. Chapter Revision Summary & Multilingual Bibliography

### Key Takeaways

- **DAG Disjoint vs. Overlapping Path Covers**: On a DAG $G = (V, E)$, $\text{MDPC}(G) = |V| - \nu(G_{\text{split}}(G))$. Allowing paths to share vertices is equivalent to taking the **transitive closure** $\text{TC}(G)$ first.
- **Dilworth's Theorem & The Transitivity Non-Overlap Lemma**: On a strict poset $\mathcal{P} = (V, \prec)$, no element $v \in V$ has both $v_{\text{out}} \in C^*$ and $v_{\text{in}} \in C^*$. Thus $A^* = \{v \in V : v_{\text{out}} \in S_{\min} \land v_{\text{in}} \notin S_{\min}\}$ constructively recovers a Maximum (Weight) Antichain.
- **Hall–Ore Duality & Flow Elimination**: By Min-Cut duality, $\nu_{a,b}(G) = \sum_{u \in L} a_u - \max_{S \subseteq L} \big(\sum_{u \in S} a_u - \sum_{v \in N(S)} b_v\big)$. When neighborhoods are contiguous intervals or $|L| \le 18$, Segment Trees and SOS DP completely eliminate explicit flow solvers.
